Only 20 units were manufactured in platinum out of the total 1,000-piece Jubilée production run, making it one of the rarest metal variants of the reference. On the secondary market, these timepieces typically command prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range. A notable auction result occurred in 2022 when a well-preserved example sold for over $800,000, reflecting its scarcity compared to the steel and gold versions.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Jubilée reference 14802ST was produced in 1992 to commemorate the 20th anniversary of the Royal Oak. Limited to 1,000 total units across all metals, the stainless steel variant comprises 700 pieces. Collectors prioritize this reference for its 39mm "Jumbo" case profile and the ultra-thin caliber 2121 movement, which features a 21-karat gold oscillating weight visible through a sapphire exhibition caseback—a first for the Royal Oak line. The dial typically features the "Petite Tapisserie" pattern with the AP logo at 12 o’clock. Secondary market prices generally fluctuate between $80,000 and $130,000 depending on condition and the presence of original accessories. A notable variant is the "Salmon" or copper-toned dial, which was produced in very limited quantities within the 14802ST run and commands a significant premium at auction, often exceeding $250,000.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Jumbo Extra-Thin reference 15202BC was produced between 2019 and 2021. This reference is distinguished by its 39mm case and integrated bracelet constructed entirely from 18k white gold, paired with a "salmon" colored dial featuring the "Petite Tapisserie" pattern. It utilizes the self-winding Calibre 2121, a movement measuring 3.05mm in thickness, which allows for an overall case profile of 8.1mm. Collectors value this specific model due to its limited production volume and the historical significance of the salmon dial, which was previously reserved for anniversary editions. On the secondary market, prices typically range between $160,000 and $220,000 depending on condition and provenance. A notable production detail is that this reference was not a limited edition by number but was restricted to Audemars Piguet boutiques, contributing to its scarcity before the 15202 series was discontinued in 2022.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Extra-Thin 15202PT was introduced in 2021 as a limited production model before the 15202 reference was discontinued in 2022. Collectors prioritize this specific iteration because it features a solid 950 platinum case and bracelet paired with a smoked green sunburst dial, a departure from the traditional "Petite Tapisserie" pattern. It houses the self-winding Calibre 2121, which measures 3.05mm in thickness, allowing for an overall case profile of 8.1mm. Unlike the steel 15202ST, the 15202PT was not a numbered limited edition but saw extremely low production volume, distributed exclusively through AP Houses. On the secondary market, prices typically range from $400,000 to $550,000 depending on condition and provenance. A notable auction result occurred at Phillips in 2021, where a unique 15202PT with a titanium case and platinum bezel sold for over $3.1 million for charity.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Extra-Thin "Only Watch" reference 15202XT.GG.1240XT.01 was produced as a unique piece for the 2021 Only Watch charity auction. This reference is distinguished by its case construction, which utilizes sandblasted titanium paired with a polished bezel and studs made of a palladium-based Bulk Metallic Glass (BMG). This marked the first time the manufacturer employed BMG, a material valued for its high resistance to scratches and corrosion. The watch features a grey "Petite Tapisserie" dial and is powered by the caliber 2121, the final instance of this movement being used in a 15202 reference before its retirement. As a unique piece, it does not have a standard secondary market price range; however, it sold at Christie’s in November 2021 for 3,100,000 CHF. This result represents one of the highest prices ever paid for a Royal Oak at auction.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak reference 15203PT was released in 2012 to commemorate the 40th anniversary of the model line. Production was limited to 40 pieces, all cased in 950 platinum. This reference utilizes the ultra-thin self-winding Calibre 2121, which was the original movement used in the 1972 Royal Oak. The 39mm case features a display caseback with a dedicated 40th-anniversary oscillating weight. Its dial is finished in a smoked grey "Petite Tapisserie" pattern with white gold applied hour markers. Collectors value this reference for its material density, historical movement, and extreme scarcity compared to the standard 15202 series. On the secondary market, prices typically reside in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often exceeding $500,000 depending on provenance. A notable auction result occurred in 2022 when a well-preserved example sold for over 800,000 CHF, reflecting its status among high-level Royal Oak collectors.

The Audemars Piguet Reference 1533 was produced in the early 1940s, with approximately nine units manufactured between 1941 and 1943. Collectors value this reference for its oversized 36mm case, which was unusually large for the era, and its use of the Valjoux-based caliber 13VZAH. The construction typically features a stainless steel mid-case paired with 18k rose gold bezels, pushers, and crowns. The dials often feature a two-tone aesthetic with tachymeter scales and baton markers. Due to the extreme rarity of vintage Audemars Piguet chronographs—of which only 307 were made between 1930 and 1950—this reference occupies a significant place in the brand's history. On the secondary market, these watches command prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range. A notable example formerly owned by Giorgio Seragnoli sold at auction in 2015 for approximately 305,000 CHF, serving as the design inspiration for the 2020 [Re]master01 release.

references.model: Royal Oak Double Balance Wheel Openworked
references.description: The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Double Balance Wheel Openworked reference 15416CE.OO.1220CE.01 was introduced in 2020 as a boutique-exclusive model and remains in limited production. This reference is distinguished by its 41mm case and integrated bracelet crafted entirely from brushed and polished black ceramic. It houses the manufacture caliber 3132, which utilizes two balance wheels and two hairsprings on the same axis to improve chronometric stability. The skeletonized dial features pink gold bridges that contrast against the dark aesthetic, with the double balance mechanism visible at the eight o'clock position. Collectors prioritize this reference due to the technical complexity of the movement combined with the high demand for ceramic Royal Oaks. On the secondary market, prices typically range from $250,000 to $350,000. A notable variant is the 15416SB, a unique piece with a blue inner bezel created for the One Night for One Drop charity auction.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak reference 15502OR is a 41mm boutique-exclusive model produced around 2019 to 2021. This reference is distinguished by its 18k pink gold construction and a "Grande Tapisserie" dial set with 466 brilliant-cut diamonds, totaling approximately 3.16 carats. It utilizes the self-winding Calibre 4302, which provides a 70-hour power reserve and operates at a frequency of 4 Hz. Collectors value this reference for its integration of high-jewelry techniques with the standard 15500 case architecture, offering a more substantial presence than the 37mm gem-set variants. On the secondary market, this reference typically trades in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often between $150,000 and $220,000 depending on condition and provenance. A notable production detail is its limited distribution through official boutiques, making it significantly rarer than the standard non-gem-set 15500OR models.

The Audemars Piguet reference 16869, often referred to as the Grosse Pièce, was produced in the early 1990s as a limited series of approximately 50 units. Collectors value this reference for its oversized 40mm 18k yellow gold case, which was unusually large for the era, and its use of the caliber 2120/2802. This ultra-thin automatic movement features a perpetual calendar with a leap year indicator and a moon phase. The dial typically features a white porcelain-like finish with recessed sub-dials and stick markers. Due to its limited production run and historical significance as a precursor to the modern oversized luxury watch trend, the reference 16869 occupies a niche position in the brand's heritage. On the secondary market, these timepieces generally command prices in the mid-to-high five-figure range, with exceptional examples occasionally reaching the low-six-figures at international auctions.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak reference 25402SA was produced during the late 1970s and early 1980s as a mid-sized alternative to the "Jumbo" models. This reference features a 33mm case constructed from stainless steel and 18k yellow gold, housing the ultra-thin quartz Calibre 2502. Collectors value this reference for its historical role in the brand’s transition during the Quartz Crisis and its adherence to the original Gerald Genta design language, including the integrated bracelet and octagonal bezel. The dial typically features the "Petite Tapisserie" pattern with an AP logo positioned at 12 o'clock. On the secondary market, the 25402SA generally trades between $12,000 and $18,000 depending on condition and the presence of original paperwork. A notable production detail is that this reference was among the first Royal Oaks to utilize a quartz movement, marking a specific era of technical experimentation for the manufacturer.

The Audemars Piguet Quantième Perpétuel reference 25548BA was produced between approximately 1982 and the early 1990s, representing a pivotal era for the brand’s ultra-thin complications. This 18k yellow gold model measures 36mm in diameter and is powered by the self-winding caliber 2120/2800, which is based on the Jaeger-LeCoultre 920 movement. Collectors value this reference for its historical significance in popularizing the perpetual calendar during the post-quartz crisis recovery and for its classic four-subdial layout without a leap year indicator. The case features a stepped bezel and short lugs, characteristic of the Quantième Perpétuel line's early design language. On the secondary market, this reference typically trades between $35,000 and $55,000 depending on condition and the presence of original paperwork. A notable production detail is that early examples often feature "Audemars Piguet" branding without the "Automatic" text on the dial, a variation sought by vintage enthusiasts.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar reference 25554ST was produced between approximately 1986 and 1991. Collectors prioritize this reference as the first Royal Oak to feature a perpetual calendar complication, marking a significant technical expansion for the model line. It utilizes the ultra-thin automatic caliber 2120/2800, derived from a Jaeger-LeCoultre base. The 39mm stainless steel case maintains the "Jumbo" proportions but lacks a leap year indicator on the dial, a characteristic of early generation perpetual calendars. Production was limited, with records suggesting fewer than 300 units were manufactured in steel. On the secondary market, these watches typically trade in the low-to-mid six-figure range depending on provenance and condition. A notable variant includes the "Yves Klein" dial, featuring a vibrant blue aesthetic, which often commands a significant premium at international auctions due to its rarity and visual distinction.

Produced between approximately 1986 and the mid-1990s, the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar Openworked reference 25636BA is a significant neo-vintage reference housed in a 39mm 18k yellow gold case. Collectors prioritize this model for its ultra-thin self-winding caliber 2120/2800, which lacks a leap year indicator, a characteristic of early perpetual calendar movements. The sapphire dial reveals the hand-finished skeletonized components, while the absence of a sapphire caseback on many early examples distinguishes it from later iterations. Total production for the 25636BA is estimated at 126 units, making it rarer than its non-skeletonized counterparts. On the secondary market, prices typically occupy the mid-to-high six-figure range, depending on the presence of the original box and papers. A notable auction result occurred in 2022 when a well-preserved example sold for over $400,000, reflecting the high demand for early openworked Royal Oaks.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar Openworked reference 25636PT was produced between approximately 1993 and 1996. Collectors prioritize this reference for its combination of a 39mm "Jumbo" ultra-thin case profile and the caliber 2120/2800, a self-winding movement featuring a hand-finished skeletonized structure. Unlike standard perpetual calendars, the 25636 lacks a leap year indicator, a characteristic of early Royal Oak complications. The platinum construction represents the rarest metal variant of this reference, with production estimated at fewer than 35 units. This scarcity, paired with the transition from the "Quantième Perpétuel" era to modern aesthetics, places secondary market values in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often exceeding $400,000 depending on provenance. A notable 2023 auction result at Phillips saw a well-preserved example achieve over $600,000, underscoring the demand for low-production platinum skeletonized Royal Oaks among high-level collectors.

Produced between 1982 and 1993, the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar reference 25654BA represents an early evolution of the ultra-thin perpetual calendar complication within the Royal Oak line. Collectors prioritize this reference for its 39mm "Jumbo" case proportions and the caliber 2120/2800, a movement derived from a Jaeger-LeCoultre base that allowed for a case thickness of approximately 8.2mm. Unlike modern iterations, the 25654BA lacks a leap year indicator on the dial, a characteristic of early AP perpetual calendars. Approximately 422 units were manufactured in 18k yellow gold. On the secondary market, these timepieces typically trade in the $100,000 to $160,000 range depending on the presence of original paperwork and dial condition. A notable variant includes the "Yves Klein" electric blue smooth dial, which commands a significant premium over the standard champagne or white tapisserie versions at international auctions.

Produced between 1982 and 1993, the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar reference 25654PT represents the platinum execution of the brand’s second-generation perpetual calendar. Collectors prioritize this reference for its ultra-thin Calibre 2120/2800 movement and the absence of a leap year indicator, which maintains a symmetrical four-subdial layout. The platinum variant is notably rare, with records indicating only 38 units were manufactured out of the total 800 pieces produced across all metals. These watches feature a 39mm "Jumbo" case construction without a sapphire caseback, adhering to traditional proportions. On the secondary market, prices typically occupy the mid-to-high six-figure range, often fluctuating between $250,000 and $500,000 depending on dial configuration. A notable production detail includes the transition from the early "MK1" dials with smaller Audemars Piguet typography to later versions, with rare "Tuscan" textured dials commanding significant premiums at major international auctions.

Produced between 1982 and 1993, the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar reference 25654SA is a two-tone execution featuring a stainless steel case and bracelet with an 18k yellow gold bezel and center links. Collectors value this reference for its ultra-thin Caliber 2120/2800 movement and its transitional status, as it lacks a leap year indicator on the dial, maintaining a symmetrical four-subdial layout. The 39mm "Jumbo" case dimensions and the absence of the "Tapisserie" pattern on many early smooth or matte dials distinguish it from later iterations. Current secondary market prices typically range from $75,000 to $110,000 depending on provenance and condition. Approximately 425 units were produced in this specific steel and gold configuration, making it rarer than the full yellow gold 25654BA. Notable examples featuring "Yves Klein" blue dials or early Mark 1 dial signatures often command premiums at international auctions.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar reference 25654ST was produced between 1982 and 1998, with approximately 429 units manufactured in stainless steel. Collectors prioritize this reference for its 39mm "Jumbo" case profile and the ultra-thin caliber 2120/2800, which lacks a leap year indicator on the dial. Unlike modern iterations, the 25654ST features a smooth, non-tapisserie dial, often found in silver or blue, and a closed caseback. Its historical significance lies in its role as a transitional model that maintained the original Genta proportions while housing a complex complication. Secondary market prices typically range from $120,000 to $180,000 depending on condition and provenance. A notable variant includes the "Yves Klein" blue dial, which commands a significant premium at auction. Production records indicate that while 800 total units were planned across all metals, the steel version remains the most sought-after for its utilitarian aesthetic.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar reference 25659BA was produced during the late 1980s and early 1990s. This 39mm 18k yellow gold model is distinguished by its factory gem-setting, typically featuring a diamond-set bezel and hour markers. It utilizes the ultra-thin automatic caliber 2120/2800, a movement derived from the Jaeger-LeCoultre 920 base. Collectors value this reference for its "Jumbo" proportions and its role in the evolution of the perpetual calendar complication within the Royal Oak line. Production numbers for gem-set variants were significantly lower than the standard 25654 or 25820 references, contributing to its scarcity. On the secondary market, these pieces generally command prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range depending on provenance and condition. A notable example featuring a "Tuscan" texture dial and factory diamonds sold at auction for over $400,000, reflecting the premium placed on rare dial configurations.

The Audemars Piguet Quantième Perpétuel reference 25668PT was produced between approximately 1989 and the mid-1990s as a skeletonized variation of the classic 25657. Collectors value this reference for its 36mm platinum case and the ultra-thin self-winding caliber 2120/2800, which features a hand-finished, openworked movement visible through sapphire crystals on both the front and back. Unlike the solid-dial versions, the 25668 utilizes transparent sub-dials for the day, date, month, and moon phase, showcasing the intricate perpetual calendar mechanism. Production was limited, with fewer than 100 units estimated in platinum. On the secondary market, this reference typically trades in the $60,000 to $90,000 range depending on provenance and condition. A notable production detail is that early examples often lack the leap year indicator, a characteristic of the caliber 2120/2800 before the movement was updated in later years.

The Audemars Piguet Quantième Perpétuel reference 25736PT was produced during the 1990s as a skeletonized execution of the brand’s ultra-thin perpetual calendar line. Collectors value this reference for its 33mm platinum case and the caliber 2120/2800, a self-winding movement based on the Jaeger-LeCoultre 920 base with a perpetual calendar module. The open-worked dial features four sub-dials for day, date, month, and moon phase, often accented by blued steel hands and white sub-dial rings for legibility. Its rarity is defined by limited production numbers compared to standard solid-dial variants. On the secondary market, this reference typically trades in the $60,000 to $90,000 range depending on the presence of the original box and papers. A notable production detail is the use of a sapphire caseback, which was a transition from the solid casebacks found on earlier 25656 or 25668 references.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar reference 25820PT was produced from the late 1990s through approximately 2012. This reference is constructed from 950 platinum, featuring a 39mm "Jumbo" case profile and an integrated bracelet. It utilizes the self-winding caliber 2120/2802, which is based on the ultra-thin Jaeger-LeCoultre 920 movement. Collectors prioritize this reference for its leap-year indicator on the dial—a feature absent from its predecessor, the 25721—and its traditional 39mm proportions. The platinum variant is significantly heavier and rarer than the steel or gold versions, often featuring a smooth "Tuscan" or a classic "Petite Tapisserie" dial. Current secondary market prices typically fall within the $150,000 to $250,000 range depending on dial configuration and condition. A notable production detail is the transition from solid casebacks to sapphire display backs during the mid-2000s, which impacts collector preference and value.

The Audemars Piguet Jules Audemars Grande Sonnerie reference 25825PT was produced during the late 1990s and early 2000s and is no longer in production. This reference is valued for its caliber 2890 movement, a manual-wind caliber featuring both grande and petite sonnerie functions alongside a carillon minute repeater with three gongs. The 39mm case is constructed from 950 platinum and typically features a white enamel dial with Breguet numerals. Collectors prioritize this reference due to its mechanical complexity and limited production, as fewer than 50 units are estimated to exist across all metal variants. On the secondary market, this reference typically commands prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range, depending on provenance and condition. A notable auction result occurred in 2016 when a platinum example sold for approximately 300,000 CHF, though current market valuations for well-maintained examples often exceed those historical benchmarks.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar Openworked reference 25829BA was produced from approximately the mid-1990s until the early 2010s. This reference is constructed in 18k yellow gold with a 39mm case diameter and a thickness of 9.3mm, maintaining the "Jumbo" proportions favored by collectors. It features the ultra-thin self-winding caliber 2120/2802, which is visible through the sapphire dial and exhibition caseback. The movement is hand-finished with extensive skeletonization and engraving on the bridges and the 21k gold rotor. Collectors value this reference for its bridge between traditional finishing and the integrated bracelet design. On the secondary market, prices typically range from $250,000 to $350,000 depending on the presence of original accessories. Production was limited, with approximately 424 units estimated to have been produced in yellow gold. A notable 2023 auction result at Phillips reached approximately $241,000 for a 1997 example.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar Openworked reference 25829OR was produced from the late 1990s through approximately 2012. This reference is valued for its 39mm "Jumbo" case proportions and the caliber 2120/2802, an ultra-thin self-winding movement visible through the sapphire dial and exhibition caseback. Unlike modern iterations, the 25829OR features a hand-finished skeletonized architecture and traditional leap year indicators without a week display. The 18k pink gold construction was produced in limited quantities compared to steel or tantalum versions, contributing to its scarcity. On the secondary market, this reference typically trades in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often between $250,000 and $450,000 depending on provenance and condition. A notable auction result occurred in 2022 when a well-preserved example sold for over $600,000, reflecting the high demand for the discontinued 39mm perpetual calendar complications within the Royal Oak lineage.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar Openworked reference 25829ST was produced from approximately 1997 through 2014. Collectors prioritize this reference for its ultra-thin caliber 2120/2802, which measures 4mm in thickness and features a hand-finished skeletonized movement visible through sapphire crystals on both sides. The 39mm stainless steel case maintains the "Jumbo" proportions favored by purists, distinguishing it from later 41mm iterations. Production numbers were limited, with estimates suggesting fewer than 1,000 units were manufactured in steel over its seventeen-year run. On the secondary market, this reference typically commands prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often fluctuating between $250,000 and $450,000 depending on provenance and condition. A notable production detail is the transition from the "straight" Audemars Piguet logo to the curved "Audemars Piguet & Co" script on the rotor, a nuance often used to date specific examples within the production cycle.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar Openworked reference 25829TP was produced from the late 1990s through the mid-2010s. Collectors prioritize this reference for its rare bi-metal construction, combining a tantalum case and bracelet links with a 950 platinum bezel and center links. The 39mm "Jumbo" case houses the ultra-thin self-winding caliber 2120/2802, visible through a sapphire dial that displays the perpetual calendar functions without obscuring the skeletonized movement. Production numbers for the TP variant are significantly lower than the steel or gold versions, with estimates suggesting fewer than 100 units were manufactured. On the secondary market, this reference typically commands prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often exceeding $400,000 depending on provenance. A notable 2023 auction result at Phillips saw a well-preserved example achieve approximately $480,000, reflecting the high demand for tantalum Royal Oaks among specialized collectors.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar Openworked reference 25829TR was produced from the late 1990s through the mid-2010s. This reference is distinguished by its bi-metal construction, pairing a tantalum case and outer bracelet links with 18k pink gold bezels and center links. Collectors prioritize this model for its skeletonized caliber 2120/2802, an ultra-thin automatic movement visible through the sapphire dial and exhibition caseback. The use of tantalum, a dense and difficult-to-machine refractory metal, makes this variant significantly rarer than standard steel or gold iterations. Current secondary market valuations typically fall within the $250,000 to $400,000 range depending on condition and provenance. Production records suggest that fewer than 100 units of the 25829TR were manufactured, and a notable example sold at a Phillips auction in 2021 for approximately 302,000 CHF, confirming its status as a low-volume collector piece.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Automatique Tourbillon reference 25831ST was produced in 1997 to commemorate the 25th anniversary of the Royal Oak. This stainless steel model features a 39mm case and is powered by the caliber 2875, an automatic movement that positions the tourbillon carriage at 6 o'clock and the power reserve indicator at 9 o'clock. Collectors value this reference for its historical significance as the first Royal Oak to feature a tourbillon visible through the dial and its limited production of only 25 pieces. The dial lacks the traditional Tapisserie pattern, utilizing a smooth finish with a date sub-dial at 3 o'clock. On the secondary market, this reference typically commands prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range. A notable auction result occurred in 2022 when a 25831ST sold for approximately $500,000, reflecting its rarity and status among high-complication steel sport watches.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Offshore Perpetual Calendar reference 25854TI was produced during the late 1990s and early 2000s. Collectors target this reference for its 42mm titanium construction, which offers a lighter alternative to the heavier steel and gold variants of the era. It is powered by the self-winding caliber 2120/2802, a movement based on the ultra-thin JLC 920 ebauche integrated with a perpetual calendar module. The dial typically features the "Petite Tapisserie" pattern with four sub-dials indicating day, date, month, leap year, and moon phase. Due to limited production numbers, these pieces appear infrequently on the secondary market, generally commanding prices in the $60,000 to $90,000 range depending on condition and provenance. A notable variant includes the 25854ST in stainless steel, though the titanium 25854TI remains distinct for its specific matte finish and weight profile.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Offshore T3, reference 25863TI, was released in 2003 as a limited edition of 1,000 pieces to coincide with the film Terminator 3: Rise of the Machines. This reference is distinguished by its oversized 48mm titanium case, which was the largest Offshore produced at the time of its debut. It features protective crown guards and a Méga Tapisserie dial housing the caliber 2226/2840 modular chronograph movement. Collectors value the T3 for its role in establishing the trend for oversized luxury sports watches and its association with Arnold Schwarzenegger. On the secondary market, prices typically range from $30,000 to $45,000 depending on the presence of the original presentation box and papers. Of the 1,000 units produced, 500 were configured with a silver dial and 500 with a black dial, both featuring Arabic numerals and a tachymeter scale.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Grand Complication reference 25865BC was produced primarily during the late 1990s and 2000s. This 44mm 18k white gold timepiece houses the caliber 2885, a self-winding movement composed of 648 parts. It integrates three traditional high complications: a minute repeater, a perpetual calendar, and a split-seconds chronograph. Collectors prioritize this reference for its technical density and the hand-finished nature of its movement, which includes a solid gold oscillating weight and a chime sequence struck on two gongs. The dial typically features a silvered "Grande Tapisserie" pattern with white gold applied hour markers. On the secondary market, this reference generally commands prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often between $450,000 and $700,000 depending on provenance. A notable production detail is that each unit required over 600 hours of assembly by a single master watchmaker at the brand’s Grandes Complications workshop.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Grande Complication reference 25865ST was introduced in the late 1990s and remained in limited production through the 2010s. This reference is defined by the caliber 2885, a hand-finished movement comprising 648 parts that integrates a minute repeater, perpetual calendar, and split-seconds chronograph. Collectors prioritize the 25865ST for its 44mm stainless steel case, a rare material choice for a high-complication timepiece typically reserved for precious metals. The dial features a traditional white tapisserie pattern with four sub-dials and a moon phase indicator. Due to the complexity of the movement, production was limited to very few units per year. On the secondary market, this reference typically commands prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often between $450,000 and $700,000 depending on provenance. A notable 2021 auction result saw a well-preserved example achieve over $600,000, reflecting its status as a pinnacle of the Royal Oak line.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Grande Complication reference 25990BC was introduced in the late 1990s and remained in production through the 2010s as a pinnacle of the brand’s technical catalog. This reference features a 44mm case crafted from 18k white gold, housing the self-winding caliber 2885. The movement integrates three traditional high complications: a minute repeater, a perpetual calendar with moon phase, and a split-seconds chronograph. Collectors value this reference for its complexity and the hand-finished nature of its 648 components. The dial typically features the signature Petite Tapisserie pattern with silvered sub-dials. On the secondary market, these timepieces generally command prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often between $450,000 and $700,000 depending on condition and provenance. A notable 2021 auction result at Phillips saw a white gold example achieve approximately $500,000, underscoring the sustained demand for these low-volume production pieces.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Offshore Alinghi Team Chronograph, reference 26062OR.OO.A002CA.01, was released in 2007 as a limited edition of 600 pieces to commemorate the 32nd America’s Cup. This reference features a 44mm case constructed from 18k rose gold paired with a forged carbon bezel, a material innovation pioneered by the brand during this era. It utilizes the caliber 2326/2848 self-winding movement, which includes a specialized ten-minute regatta countdown function displayed on the dial. The aesthetic is defined by a black "Méga Tapisserie" pattern with red accents and the Alinghi logo at the 3 o'clock position. On the secondary market, this reference typically trades between $35,000 and $50,000 depending on condition and the presence of original packaging. While the forged carbon and rose gold combination is the primary production variant, the collection also included versions in full forged carbon and platinum.

The Audemars Piguet Edward Piguet Tourbillon Grande Date reference 26119BC was produced during the mid-2000s and is no longer in current production. This reference is valued for its rectangular 18k white gold case, which measures 29mm by 49mm, and its integration of a tourbillon with a large date complication. It houses the manual-wind caliber 2891, a movement featuring a 70-hour power reserve and a visible tourbillon carriage at the six o'clock position. The dial typically features a silvered finish with guilloché patterns and applied Arabic numerals. Collectors monitor this reference due to its limited production numbers compared to the Royal Oak line. On the secondary market, this model generally trades in the $40,000 to $65,000 range depending on condition and provenance. A notable variant includes the reference 26009BC, which shares the case silhouette but utilizes the caliber 2886 with a power reserve indicator.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Offshore reference 26170ST was produced from approximately 2005 until 2014. Collectors prioritize this reference for its 42mm stainless steel case and the use of the Calibre 3126/3840 modular chronograph movement, which replaced the earlier Calibre 2226/2841. This reference is noted for its "Méga Tapisserie" dial and the transition from rubber-clad pushers and crowns to black ceramic components in later production years. It represents the definitive mid-era aesthetic of the Offshore collection before the introduction of the 44mm models and integrated ceramic bezels. On the secondary market, prices typically range between $18,000 and $26,000 depending on the specific dial configuration and condition. A notable variant is the "Safari" execution, distinguished by its cream-colored dial and brown hornback alligator strap, which remains one of the most recognizable iterations of the 26170ST series.

references.model: Royal Oak Concept Laptimer Michael Schumacher
references.description: Released in 2015 as a limited edition of 221 pieces, the Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Concept Laptimer Michael Schumacher (reference 26221FT.OO.D002CA.01) is no longer in production. Collectors prioritize this reference for its unique Calibre 2923 movement, which features a world-first mechanical complication: a double-chronograph system capable of measuring consecutive lap times with a single flyback and restart function. The 44mm case is constructed from forged carbon with a titanium bezel and caseback, housing a skeletonized dial that reveals the column-wheel mechanisms. This model represents a five-year collaboration between the manufacturer and the Formula 1 driver. On the secondary market, this reference typically commands prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often between $600,000 and $850,000 depending on condition. A notable auction result occurred in 2022 when a well-preserved example sold for approximately $750,000, reflecting its rarity and technical complexity.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Tourbillon Extra-Thin reference 26511PT was introduced around 2012 as a limited production model and is no longer in the current catalog. This reference is distinguished by its 41mm case and integrated bracelet constructed entirely from 950 platinum, making it significantly heavier than steel or titanium counterparts. It houses the manual-wind Calibre 2924, which measures 4.46mm thick and provides a 70-hour power reserve. The dial features a blue "Petite Tapisserie" pattern with a visible tourbillon cage at the six o'clock position. Collectors value this reference for its combination of a high-complication movement with the density of platinum and its limited availability compared to standard gold models. On the secondary market, this reference typically trades in the mid-to-high six-figure range. A notable variant includes the 26511TR, which utilizes a bi-metal construction of titanium and ruthenium.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Tourbillon Extra-Thin Openworked reference 26518ST.OO.1220ST.01 was introduced in 2017 as a limited edition of 100 pieces. This reference is valued for its combination of a stainless steel case and bracelet with a skeletonized tourbillon movement, a pairing typically reserved for precious metals or titanium. It houses the manual-wind Calibre 2924, which measures 4.46mm thick, allowing for a total case height of 8.95mm. The openworked architecture features slate grey bridges and a visible mainspring barrel at the one o'clock position. On the secondary market, this reference typically trades in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often between $450,000 and $650,000 depending on condition and provenance. A notable auction result occurred in 2021 when a specimen sold for approximately $770,000, reflecting the scarcity of steel-cased complications within the Royal Oak lineage compared to their gold counterparts.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar reference 26579CE.OO.1225CE.01 entered production in 2017 and remains a centerpiece of the brand’s contemporary catalog. Collectors prioritize this reference for its full black ceramic construction, including the case, bezel, and integrated bracelet, which requires over 600 hours of finishing to achieve the signature brushed and polished surfaces. It features a "Grande Tapisserie" dial with four sub-dials, including a photorealistic moon phase and a week indicator on the outer chapter ring. Powering the watch is the ultra-thin self-winding Calibre 5134, based on the historic Calibre 2120. On the secondary market, prices typically fluctuate within the $225,000 to $300,000 range depending on condition and provenance. A notable variant is the "White Ceramic" 26579CB, though the black ceramic remains the foundational application of this material for the perpetual calendar complication within the Royal Oak collection.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Perpetual Calendar Openworked reference 26585CE.OO.1225CE.01 was introduced in 2019 and remains in the current catalog as a boutique-exclusive model. Collectors prioritize this reference for its full black ceramic construction, including the case, bezel, and integrated bracelet, which requires high labor intensity to finish. It houses the self-winding caliber 5135, a skeletonized movement visible through a sapphire dial that features smoked external zones and pink gold applied hour markers. The secondary market price for this reference typically ranges between $375,000 and $450,000, though it reached significantly higher peaks in 2022. A notable production detail is the use of a titanium folding clasp for durability against the ceramic links. In 2021, a unique "Cactus Jack" collaboration variant was released, but the standard 26585CE remains the foundational high-complication ceramic model for the brand.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Concept Supersonnerie reference 26591IO.OO.A002CA.01 was introduced in 2016 and remains a low-volume production piece within the brand’s high-complication catalog. Collectors prioritize this reference for its caliber 2937 movement, which utilizes a patented soundboard technology and a unique striking mechanism designed to amplify the minute repeater’s chime. The 44mm case is constructed from sandblasted titanium with a black ceramic bezel, screw-locked crown, and pushpieces. Its openworked dial features a black 30-minute counter and yellow accents for legibility. This reference represents the commercial application of the RD#1 prototype, focusing on acoustic performance in a water-resistant case. On the secondary market, this model typically commands prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often between $350,000 and $550,000 depending on condition. A notable production detail is the caseback’s "sonic" perforations, which allow sound to escape while maintaining 20-meter water resistance.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Grand Complication reference 26605CE.OO.1248CE.01 was introduced in 2019 and remains a limited-production piece within the current catalog. This reference features a 44mm case and integrated bracelet crafted entirely from brushed and polished black ceramic. It houses the self-winding Calibre 2885, a movement composed of 648 parts that integrates three traditional high complications: a minute repeater, a perpetual calendar, and a split-seconds chronograph. The sapphire dial provides a view of the movement architecture, including the hammers and gongs. Due to the technical difficulty of finishing ceramic and the complexity of the movement, production is extremely limited, often cited at fewer than ten units annually. On the secondary market, this reference typically commands prices in the high-six-figure to low-seven-figure range. A similar open-worked ceramic execution reached approximately 800,000 USD at auction, reflecting its position as a pinnacle technical offering.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Concept Flying Tourbillon reference 26623TI.GG.D002CA.01 was introduced in 2021 and remains in the current catalog. This reference is distinguished by its 44mm sandblasted titanium case and a multi-layered dial featuring a hand-wound manufacture caliber 2964. Collectors value this model for its technical integration of a flying tourbillon and a power reserve indicator, alongside the circular graining motif on the bridges that is visible through the sapphire dial and caseback. The movement provides a 72-hour power reserve and operates at 3 Hz. On the secondary market, this reference typically commands prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often fluctuating between $170,000 and $230,000 depending on condition and provenance. A notable production detail is the use of green CVD accents on the movement bridges, a specific aesthetic departure from the traditional monochromatic finishes found in earlier Concept iterations.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Selfwinding Flying Tourbillon reference 26730BC.GG.1320BC.01 was introduced in 2022 to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the Royal Oak. This 41mm reference features an 18k white gold case and bracelet finished with a hammered "Frosted Gold" technique. It houses the manufacture caliber 2950, a selfwinding movement with a 65-hour power reserve and a flying tourbillon visible at six o'clock. The dial is characterized by a blue "Dimpled" texture rather than the traditional Tapisserie pattern. While the 50th-anniversary edition featured a dedicated oscillating weight, subsequent production continues without the anniversary branding. On the secondary market, this reference typically commands prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often between $450,000 and $600,000 depending on the specific dial execution and provenance. A notable 2022 auction result for a 50th-anniversary variant reached approximately $630,000, reflecting the premium placed on the initial commemorative production run.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak Selfwinding Flying Tourbillon reference 26730OR.OO.1320OR.01 was introduced in 2022 to commemorate the 50th anniversary of the Royal Oak and remains in current production. This reference features a 41mm case and integrated bracelet crafted from 18k pink gold, housing the manufacture caliber 2950. Collectors value this model for its combination of a flying tourbillon complication with a central rotor, a departure from previous hand-wound tourbillon iterations. The dial utilizes a "Grande Tapisserie" pattern in smoked blue, transitioning to black at the periphery. For the 2022 production year, the movement features a specific "50 Years" oscillating weight, a detail absent in subsequent years. On the secondary market, this reference typically trades in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often between $180,000 and $240,000 depending on the production year and condition. A notable 2022 example sold at auction for over $250,000.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak reference 4100BA was produced from the late 1970s through the 1980s as the first mid-sized execution of the model line. Collectors target this 18k yellow gold reference for its 35mm case diameter, which offers a traditional alternative to the larger "Jumbo" proportions. It features the self-winding Calibre 2123, a movement derived from the Jaeger-LeCoultre 889. The construction includes an integrated bracelet and a monobloc case design consistent with the original Gérald Genta aesthetic. Most examples feature the "Petite Tapisserie" dial pattern with an applied AP logo at 12 o'clock. On the secondary market, the 4100BA typically trades between $35,000 and $55,000 depending on condition and the presence of original paperwork. A notable production detail is the transition from "Audemars Piguet" script to the block logo on later dials, which influences specific collector preferences for early-series aesthetics.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak reference 5402 in stainless steel and 18k yellow gold was produced during the mid-to-late 1970s and early 1980s. Collectors value this reference as the original "Jumbo" execution, featuring the ultra-thin Calibre 2121 movement and a 39mm monobloc case construction. This specific two-tone configuration is historically significant because it includes Gérald Genta’s personal timepiece, which he customized with a unique 18k gold bezel. The dial typically features the "Petite Tapisserie" pattern with the "AP" logo positioned at 6 o’clock on earlier A-series and B-series examples. On the secondary market, standard two-tone 5402 models generally trade between $40,000 and $80,000 depending on condition and provenance. A notable auction result occurred in 2022 when Genta’s personal 5402 sold for approximately $2.1 million, establishing a record for the reference and highlighting the premium placed on unique historical ownership.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak reference 5402BA was produced from 1977 through the early 1980s as the first precious metal iteration of the original Jumbo design. Collectors prioritize this reference for its 39mm "Jumbo" monobloc case construction and the ultra-thin Calibre 2121 automatic movement. Unlike modern solid gold versions, the 5402BA features a specific vintage aesthetic defined by its "Petite Tapisserie" dial and a thinner profile than later iterations. Production was limited, with approximately 736 units manufactured, making it significantly rarer than its steel counterpart. On the secondary market, prices typically range from $120,000 to over $200,000 depending on the presence of the "A-series" serial number or original paperwork. A notable production detail is the existence of the "Jubilee" variant or pieces with the "AP" logo at six o'clock, which command premiums at international auctions due to their proximity to the original 1972 design layout.

The Audemars Piguet Royal Oak 5402ST A-Series was produced between 1972 and approximately 1974, representing the first 2,000 units of the original Royal Oak production. Collectors prioritize the A-Series due to its historical status as the debut luxury steel sports watch and its specific design features, including the "AP" logo positioned at 6 o'clock rather than 12 o'clock. The reference features a 39mm monobloc case and the ultra-thin Calibre 2121, developed by Jaeger-LeCoultre. Secondary market prices typically fall within the $100,000 to $200,000 range, though exceptional examples with original "tropical" dials or full sets can exceed these figures. A notable production detail is the sequential numbering on the case back; collectors specifically seek the earliest "A-Series" designations, as later B, C, and D series moved the logo to the 12 o'clock position and saw higher production volumes.

references.model: Perpetual Calendar with Leap Year Indication
references.description: Audemars Piguet produced the reference 5516 between 1955 and 1957, with a total production of only 12 units. This reference is historically significant as the first perpetual calendar wristwatch to feature a leap year indicator on the dial. The 36.5mm 18k yellow gold case houses the caliber 13VZSSQP, a manual-wind movement based on a Valjoux ebauche. Collectors distinguish between two primary dial configurations: the first three pieces featured the moon phase at 12 o’clock, while the subsequent nine units placed the moon phase at 6 o’clock with the leap year cycle at 12 o’clock. Due to its extreme rarity and technical importance, the reference 5516 commands prices in the high-six-figure to low-seven-figure range. A notable example sold at auction in 2015 for over $540,000, though current market valuations for well-preserved specimens often exceed $1,000,000.

The Blancpain 1735 Grande Complication was produced between 1991 and approximately 2002 as a limited edition of 30 pieces. Collectors value this reference for its caliber 1735 movement, which integrates a perpetual calendar, moon phase, split-seconds chronograph, tourbillon, and minute repeater. The 42mm case is constructed from platinum and houses 740 individual components within a movement measuring only 11mm in thickness. This reference represents the culmination of Blancpain’s "six masterpieces" project initiated after the quartz crisis to demonstrate the viability of mechanical watchmaking. On the secondary market, these timepieces typically command prices in the mid-to-high six-figure range, often appearing between $400,000 and $800,000 depending on provenance. A notable production detail is that each watch required one year of assembly by a single master watchmaker. In 2014, a well-preserved example sold at auction for approximately $470,000, reflecting its status as one of the most complex wristwatches of its era.

Released in 2003 to commemorate the model's half-century milestone, the Blancpain Fifty Fathoms 50th Anniversary Reference 2200A-1130-71 was produced in three limited series of 50 pieces each, totaling 150 units. This reference is significant to collectors as it bridged the gap between vintage aesthetics and modern specifications, introducing the sapphire crystal bezel insert that became a brand standard. The 40.3mm stainless steel case houses the automatic Calibre 1151, offering a 100-hour power reserve. The dial features a date window at 4:30 and "71" style metal bracelet or rubber strap options. On the secondary market, these watches typically trade between $25,000 and $35,000 depending on set completeness. A notable production detail is the division into Series I, II, and III, which were allocated to the Asian, European, and American markets respectively, though the technical specifications across all three series remain identical.

The Blancpain Fifty Fathoms Barakuda Only Watch reference 5008C-1130-B64A is a unique piece produced in 2019 specifically for the Only Watch charity auction. This stainless steel diver features a 40.3mm case and is powered by the automatic caliber 1151, which provides a 100-hour power reserve via two series-coupled barrels. Distinguishing it from the standard 500-piece limited edition Barakuda, this unique execution utilizes white Super-LumiNova for the hour markers and handset, which glows blue, rather than the "old radium" beige lume found on the commercial version. The dial also features a date window at 3 o'clock and a unidirectional sapphire bezel. At the 2019 Only Watch auction in Geneva, this specific timepiece sold for 45,000 CHF. Because it is a unique piece, it does not have a standard secondary market price range, though its value is tied to its status as a one-of-one prototype-style variant.

references.model: Tribute to Fifty Fathoms No Rad Only Watch
references.description: The Blancpain Tribute to Fifty Fathoms No Rad Only Watch reference 5008E-1130-B64A is a unique piece produced specifically for the 2021 Only Watch charity auction. This 40.3mm stainless steel diver distinguishes itself from the standard 500-piece "No Rad" limited edition through its orange-tinted Super-LumiNova on the hands, indices, and bezel scale, replacing the traditional beige "old radium" look. It features a matte black dial with the crossed-out radioactivity symbol and is powered by the caliber 1151 automatic movement, offering a 100-hour power reserve via two series-coupled barrels. The case includes a sapphire crystal insert on the unidirectional bezel and is water-resistant to 300 meters. While the standard production model typically trades between $25,000 and $35,000, this specific unique reference sold at Christie’s in November 2021 for 130,000 CHF. It remains a one-of-one specimen, making it unavailable for general secondary market acquisition.

references.model: Fifty Fathoms 70th Anniversary Act 1 Only Watch
references.description: The Blancpain Fifty Fathoms 70th Anniversary Act 1, reference 5010-1130-NABA, was released in 2023 as a limited production of 210 units, divided into three series of 70 for different global regions. Collectors prioritize this reference for its 42.3mm stainless steel case, a reduction from the standard 45mm Fifty Fathoms, and its use of the caliber 1315 automatic movement with a five-day power reserve. The dial features a black sunburst finish with vintage-style luminous markers and a sapphire bezel insert. On the secondary market, these watches typically trade between $25,000 and $35,000. While this specific reference was a commercial release, it shares its 42mm architecture with the unique 2023 "Only Watch" edition, which featured a blue dial and sold at auction for 160,000 CHF, signaling high demand for the mid-sized steel case format within the brand's modern catalog.

Released in 2003 to commemorate the model's 1953 debut, the Blancpain Fifty Fathoms 50th Anniversary (Ref. 2200-1130-71) was limited to 150 units across three series of 50 pieces each. This reference marked the transition of the Fifty Fathoms into the modern era, featuring a 40.3mm stainless steel case and a sapphire crystal bezel insert, which replaced the acrylic used in vintage iterations. It is powered by the Calibre 1151 automatic movement, providing a 100-hour power reserve. Collectors prioritize this reference for its specific dimensions, as it remains smaller than the subsequent 45mm standard production models. On the secondary market, these timepieces typically trade between $25,000 and $35,000 depending on the presence of the original dive light and specialized packaging. While the three series are technically identical, the case backs are individually numbered 1/50 for each specific market allocation.

The Blancpain Villeret Perpetual Calendar reference 6056-3642-53B was introduced in the early 2000s and is no longer in current production. Collectors target this reference for its 38mm 18k pink gold case and the caliber 5653 automatic movement, which provides a 100-hour power reserve. The dial features an opaline finish with applied Roman numerals and a moon phase indicator at six o'clock. A defining technical feature is the inclusion of under-lug correctors, allowing the wearer to adjust calendar indications by hand without specialized tools. On the secondary market, this reference typically trades between $18,000 and $24,000 depending on the presence of original accessories. While the 6056 series was produced in various metals, the pink gold execution is noted for its traditional aesthetic alignment with the Villeret collection's heritage. This model preceded the larger 40mm and 42mm iterations currently found in the brand's catalog.

The Blancpain Villeret Quantième Complet reference 6263-3642-55B is a 38mm complete calendar moonphase timepiece cased in 18k pink gold. This reference was introduced in the early 2000s and remained a staple of the Villeret collection for over a decade before being superseded by larger 40mm iterations. Collectors value this model for its traditional proportions and the caliber 6763 automatic movement, which provides a 100-hour power reserve. The dial features an opaline finish with applied Roman numerals and the signature "smiling" moonphase indicator at six o'clock. Unlike later versions featuring under-lug correctors, this reference utilizes recessed pushers on the case flanks for calendar adjustments. On the secondary market, this reference typically trades between $9,000 and $13,000 depending on the presence of the original box and papers. A notable production detail is the use of a stepped "double pomme" bezel, a hallmark of the Villeret design language.

The Blancpain Fifty Fathoms Milspec 1 was produced during the late 1950s and 1960s following the initial 1953 release of the standard Fifty Fathoms. Collectors prioritize this reference for its functional moisture indicator located at six o'clock, a circular disk designed to change color from blue to pink if water entered the 41mm stainless steel case. It typically houses the automatic Caliber AS 1361 or the upgraded Caliber R.310. This reference is historically significant as it met the rigorous technical specifications of the United States Navy Experimental Diving Unit. On the secondary market, authentic examples generally command prices between $80,000 and $150,000 depending on condition and provenance. A notable variant is the "US Navy" signed dial, which is particularly rare; a well-preserved Milspec 1 with this distinction achieved a sale price of approximately $125,000 at a 2021 Phillips auction.

The Blancpain Villeret Tourbillon in 18k gold, specifically the long-running Reference 6025, was introduced in the late 1990s and remained a catalog staple through the 2010s. Collectors prioritize this reference for the Caliber 25, an ultra-slim automatic movement featuring an eight-day power reserve and an off-center flying tourbillon at 12 o'clock. The 38mm case utilizes a double-stepped bezel design characteristic of the Villeret collection, often paired with a white grand feu enamel dial and painted Roman numerals. Secondary market prices typically range from $35,000 to $55,000 depending on the specific gold alloy and set completeness. A notable variant is the "Squelette" version, which features extensive hand-skeletonization of the bridges and mainplate. While production numbers were not strictly limited, the manual labor required for the movement finishing resulted in low annual output throughout its production cycle.

The Bovet Apple-Form Verge Watch, reference 663, was produced circa 1820-1830 during the brand’s early expansion into the Chinese market. Collectors value this reference for its fruit-shaped case construction, featuring 18k gold and translucent red guilloché enamel over an engine-turned ground. The movement is a fire-gilded brass verge caliber with a fusee and chain, typical of the Fleurier style intended for export. The white enamel dial includes Roman numerals and gold spade hands, protected by a hinged cover. On the secondary market, these timepieces typically command prices in the mid-five-figure to low-six-figure range depending on enamel preservation. A notable auction result occurred at Christie’s in 2013, where a similar apple-form Bovet realized approximately $150,000. These watches are often found in pairs, as was the custom for the Qing dynasty imperial court, though single examples remain highly sought after for their mechanical and decorative condition.

The Bovet Amadeo Fleurier Virtuoso VII reference ACQPR008-100 in 18k white gold was introduced around 2015 and remains a cornerstone of the brand’s Complications collection. Collectors prioritize this reference for the Caliber 16BM02AI-HSMR, a hand-wound movement featuring a perpetual calendar and a double-sided display. The 43.3mm Amadeo convertible case allows the wearer to transform the timepiece into a pocket watch, table clock, or reversible wristwatch without tools. The dial architecture utilizes a skeletonized aesthetic with offset sub-dials and a five-day power reserve indicator. Production is limited by the complexity of the movement, with few examples appearing annually. On the secondary market, this reference typically commands prices in the $45,000 to $75,000 range, depending on condition and provenance. A notable technical detail is the patented coaxial seconds mechanism, which allows the seconds hand to be displayed on both sides of the movement despite rotating in opposite directions.

The Bovet Fleurier Amadeo AF43003 in 18k pink gold is a core component of the Amadeo convertible system, introduced around 2010 and remaining a staple of the brand’s modern catalog. Collectors prioritize this reference for its patented case architecture, which allows the wearer to transform the timepiece into a pocket watch, table clock, or reversible wristwatch without tools. This specific model features the caliber 11BA12, a self-winding movement with a 72-hour power reserve. The dial typically showcases Bovet’s signature Fleurisanne engraving or grand feu enamel, often with an offset sub-dial at 12 o’clock. On the secondary market, this reference generally trades between $18,000 and $28,000 depending on condition and provenance. A notable production detail is the inclusion of a gold-plated chain, ensuring the watch functions as a complete horological set. Higher auction results are occasionally seen for examples featuring bespoke miniature paintings.

The Bovet Amadeo Fleurier 46 Tourbillon Orbis Mundi, reference AIOM004-01, was introduced around 2014 and remains a representative example of the brand’s convertible case design. Collectors prioritize this reference for the Amadeo system, which allows the 18k white gold 46mm case to function as a wristwatch, pocket watch, or desk clock without tools. The manual-wind caliber 13BM01TM-WRI features a seven-day power reserve and a patented double-face tourbillon. The dial side displays a world time function with twenty-four city indications and a power reserve indicator, while the reverse side showcases the movement architecture. Production numbers are low due to the complexity of the hand-finishing. On the secondary market, this reference typically trades in the low-to-mid six-figure range, often between $120,000 and $180,000 depending on condition. A notable variant includes the "Braveheart" tourbillon, which shares the Amadeo architecture but utilizes a different escapement.

The Bovet Pininfarina Cambiano Chronograph CHPIN001 was introduced around 2011 as a collaboration between the Swiss manufacture and the Italian design house. Collectors value this reference for its Amadeo convertible case system, which allows the 45mm stainless steel timepiece to function as a wristwatch, pocket watch, desk clock, or dashboard timer without tools. It features the caliber 13BA01, an automatic movement with a 42-hour power reserve, housed in a "bullhead" configuration with the crown and chronograph pushers at 12 o'clock. The dial utilizes vertical brushing and circular sub-dials inspired by automotive instrumentation. While Bovet maintains low annual production volumes, this reference is currently available on the secondary market for approximately $12,000 to $18,000. A notable variant is the limited edition "60th Anniversary" model, though the standard CHPIN001 remains the foundational entry in the Pininfarina partnership.

The Bovet Butterfly Tourbillon reference CP0016 was produced during the mid-2010s as part of the Fleurier collection. This 18k pink gold model features the caliber 13BA01, a hand-wound movement with a seven-day power reserve. Collectors focus on the Amadeo convertible case system, which allows the 45mm timepiece to function as a wristwatch, pocket watch, or desk clock without tools. The dial is characterized by a symmetrical layout featuring a flying tourbillon at 6 o’clock and a decorative butterfly motif integrated into the bridge work. Due to the high level of hand-finishing and limited annual production volumes, these pieces are rare on the secondary market. Current market values typically fall within the $60,000 to $95,000 range depending on condition and provenance. A notable production detail is the use of a chain-driven power reserve indicator, a technical signature of Bovet’s high-complication manufacturing.

The Bovet Récital 17 Dimier Orbis Mundi, specifically the 18k pink gold reference featuring the D505 caliber, was introduced around 2015 as part of the Dimier collection. Collectors prioritize this reference for its triple time zone complication and the integration of a high-frequency tourbillon with a seven-day power reserve. The 45mm case houses a complex dial displaying a local time sub-dial at 12 o’clock, flanked by two secondary time zone displays with 24-city discs and day/night indicators. Unlike the brand’s "Amadeo" convertible cases, the Dimier series utilizes a traditional lug architecture. On the secondary market, these timepieces typically trade between $60,000 and $95,000 depending on condition and provenance. A notable production detail is the limited nature of these movements, as Bovet manufactures the hairsprings and components in-house, often limiting specific dial configurations to small batches or unique commissions.

The Bovet Fleurier D810.0, cased in 18k white gold, was produced during the early to mid-2000s as part of the brand’s modern revival under Pascal Raffy. Collectors target this reference for its integration of the caliber 13BA08, an automatic movement featuring a perpetual calendar and a serpentine hand for the date. The 40mm case utilizes the signature Fleurier "bow" at twelve o'clock, mimicking 19th-century pocket watches, while the dial often features white lacquer or guilloché finishes with blued steel screws and hands. Due to low production volumes typical of Bovet, these pieces appear infrequently on the secondary market. Current market values generally fluctuate between $12,000 and $18,000 depending on the presence of the original white gold buckle and service history. A notable variant includes the D810.0 with a mother-of-pearl dial, which occasionally commands a premium at international auction houses.

references.model: Unique White Gold and Diamond-Set Wristwatch
references.description: The Bovet HMS5002-SD12 is a contemporary reference from the Fleurier collection, characterized by its 18k white gold 42mm case and the brand’s signature "bow" crown protector at the 12 o'clock position. Collectors value this reference for its hand-engraved movement and the integration of high-jewelry elements, featuring a bezel and bow set with round-cut diamonds. The dial typically showcases Bovet’s traditional aesthetic with Roman numerals and serpentine hands, powered by a manual-wind mechanical movement with a significant power reserve. This specific reference is produced in limited quantities, reflecting the brand's low-volume manufacturing model. On the secondary market, this model generally trades in the $25,000 to $45,000 range, depending on the total carat weight and condition. A notable aspect of this series is the convertible "Amadeo" system found in similar Fleurier models, though the HMS5002-SD12 focuses on a fixed, diamond-set wrist configuration.

The Bovet Fleurier Limited Edition NO in 18k gold was produced during the late 1990s and early 2000s as part of the brand’s revival under Pascal Raffy. Collectors target this reference for its signature Amadeo-style case, which features a 40mm diameter and a bow protector at the twelve o'clock position, mimicking a traditional pocket watch. The model typically houses a high-grade automatic movement based on the Frédéric Piguet 1150 caliber, often visible through a sapphire caseback. Dials frequently feature fired enamel or intricate guilloché patterns with Roman numerals and serpentine hands. On the secondary market, these gold models generally trade between $8,000 and $15,000 depending on the specific dial execution and condition. A notable production detail is the limited nature of these runs, often restricted to 100 or 200 pieces per dial configuration, ensuring low global supply for specific metal and color combinations.

The Bovet Récital 12 "Monsieur Bovet" in titanium was introduced in 2024 as a contemporary addition to the Dimier collection. Collectors value this reference for its manual-wind Caliber 13BMDR12C2, which features a single barrel providing a seven-day power reserve and a visible balance wheel at the 3 o’clock position. The 42mm case utilizes the brand’s signature "writing slope" architecture, tapering from top to bottom to improve legibility and ergonomics. The dial is characterized by an offset sub-dial available in various guilloché patterns and a power reserve indicator located at 10 o’clock. On the secondary market, these titanium models typically trade between $40,000 and $55,000 depending on condition. A notable production detail is the use of grade 5 titanium, a departure from the brand’s traditional precious metal offerings, intended to reduce weight while maintaining the structural complexity of the asymmetrical case design.

The Bovet Récital 11 reference R110001-SD1 is a contemporary production model introduced in the mid-2010s as part of the Dimier collection. This reference features a 41mm 18k pink gold "writing slope" case, characterized by an asymmetrical profile that tapers toward the wearer. Collectors value this model for the caliber 11BA13, a self-winding movement providing a 72-hour power reserve, and its high-complication aesthetic which includes an offset sub-dial and a precision moon phase indicator requiring adjustment only once every 122 years. The dial is distinguished by a circular-brushed finish and a diamond-set bezel. On the secondary market, this reference typically trades in the $25,000 to $40,000 range depending on condition. A notable production detail is the use of a translucent blue aventurine glass dial variant, which often commands a premium over the standard white or black lacquer versions.

The Bovet Récital 12 "Virtuoso IX" in titanium was introduced in 2024 as a permanent addition to the Dimier collection. Collectors prioritize this reference for its manual-wind Caliber 13BM12, which features a high-efficiency single barrel providing a seven-day power reserve. The 40mm "writing slope" case is constructed from Grade 5 titanium, measuring 9.8mm at its thickest point to improve wearability compared to previous Récital models. The dial architecture utilizes an offset sub-dial at 3 o’clock with a circular-brushed finish, exposing the balance wheel and a power reserve indicator. On the secondary market, these timepieces typically trade in the $20,000 to $30,000 range depending on condition. A notable production detail is the inclusion of the patented triple-blade folding clasp, which allows for fine adjustments to the strap length without tools, a feature specific to this contemporary generation of Bovet sports-elegant watches.

The Bovet Sportster SP0480 is a stainless steel chronograph produced during the early to mid-2000s, now discontinued. Collectors target this reference for its Fleurier-style case, which features a 40mm diameter and a "bullhead" configuration with the crown and oval chronograph pushers located at the 12 o'clock position. The watch utilizes the Caliber 13BA01, a self-winding movement based on the ETA 2894-2, modified to accommodate the vertical orientation and a central pulsometer or tachymeter scale. The dial typically features stylized oversized Arabic numerals and a symmetrical three-register layout. On the secondary market, this reference generally trades between $4,000 and $7,000 depending on condition and the presence of the original box and papers. A notable production detail is the integrated bow at 12 o'clock, which protects the crown and mimics the aesthetic of historical Bovet pocket watches while maintaining a modern sports watch utility.

The Breguet Reference 1039 is a mid-century triple calendar wristwatch produced in limited quantities during the 1950s and 1960s. Collectors prioritize this reference for its 36mm 18k yellow gold case, which features the brand’s signature coin-edge fluting and straight lugs. The dial typically displays a hand-guilloché center, Roman numerals on a brushed chapter ring, and apertures for the day and month, powered by a manual-wind Valjoux-based caliber. This reference represents the neo-classical aesthetic established by the house before the quartz crisis. On the secondary market, these timepieces generally command prices between $35,000 and $60,000 depending on provenance and condition. A notable example appeared at a 2017 Christie’s auction, where a well-preserved specimen sold for approximately $47,500. Production numbers remained low, as Breguet’s total annual output during this era was significantly more restricted than modern production levels.

The Breguet No. 1176 is a historical pocket watch completed in 1809, representing Abraham-Louis Breguet’s first four-minute tourbillon and the third tourbillon ever produced. Encased in 18k yellow gold, the watch features an échappement naturel, a power reserve indicator, and a subsidiary seconds dial. Collectors value this reference for its technical significance as the earliest tourbillon available for private acquisition, as the first two were retained by Breguet or gifted. The movement utilizes a gold gear train and a specialized chronometer escapement. While not a modern production reference, its historical provenance places it at the apex of the secondary market; it last appeared publicly at auction in 2014, where it realized a price of approximately 821,000 CHF. This specific piece is noted for its transition from the experimental No. 169 to a functional commercial format, marking a pivotal development in nineteenth-century precision timekeeping.
